children: A foreign currency exchange shop in Chiang Mai looked like an ordinary money changer. Thai police now say it was a laundromat for scam cash, with Tether's USDT as the detergent.

Thailand's Cyber Crime Investigation Bureau disclosed on November 20, 2026 that it had dismantled the operation. Police say a wallet linked to the main suspect recorded a turnover of more than 2.7 million USDT, valued at roughly 92 million baht.
The man allegedly behind it all was not there to see the raids. He had already left the country.

According to investigators, the shop served as a front for converting proceeds from online investment scams into USDT stablecoins. The scams in question were mainly fake share schemes pushed through social media.
The flow of money, as police describe it, ran in stages. Victims sent funds into a network of 24 mule bank accounts, which then moved the cash toward brokers for conversion.
Once the money reached the shop, it was allegedly swapped into USDT. The operators reportedly took a commission of 2-3% for the service.
Four victims have so far reported losses totaling 9,435,607.97 baht, which works out to about $275,000 to $280,000. That figure covers only the people who have come forward.
The wallet data tells a much bigger story. Police said the suspect's digital wallet logged a turnover of over 2,749,566 USDT, worth about 92 million baht.
Meanwhile, the exchange shop's official books looked rather sleepy. It declared revenue of just 443,025 baht over nine months.
Police carried out the raids on November 10, 2026. They hit the currency exchange shop and a residence in Doi Saket, a district in Chiang Mai province.
The main suspect is Wenjun Feng, a 42-year-old Chinese national. He fled Thailand before officers arrived.
An arrest warrant for Feng had been issued months earlier. He is now on an immigration watchlist.
Two people were detained. The first is Feng's wife, 36-year-old Yaning Yan, who faces charges under Thailand's Foreign Business Act.
The second is Juthamas Meechai, a 35-year-old Thai national. She served as the shop's director and majority owner, and she has been charged with nominee and false-statement offenses.

The research behind the case points to a wider pattern. Transnational scam networks involving Chinese operators have been exploiting unlicensed exchanges in Thailand to launder money through digital assets.
USDT sits at the center of that pattern. Its appeal to launderers comes down to two things: deep liquidity and fast transfers that move faster than traditional banking channels.
There is an irony here worth noting. The same blockchain that makes USDT fast also makes it traceable, which is how police were able to put a figure on the wallet's turnover in the first place.
The investigation itself is not finished. Police say the case may expand to identify additional victims and more linked financial accounts.
That matters because the numbers do not yet line up neatly. Four reported victims account for under 10 million baht, while the wallet allegedly processed around 92 million baht worth of USDT.
The other open thread is Feng himself. With the alleged mastermind abroad and an arrest warrant pending, the people facing charges right now are the ones who stayed behind.

title: Thai cyber police raid Chiang Mai exchange shop tied to 2.7 million USDT wallet
